title: Taming pain: the development of anaesthesia
dek: From Ice Age surgery with no record of pain relief to herbal and then chemical anaesthesia, reached independently in Japan and the United States.

steps.note: Surgery long predates any record of anaesthesia. How this Ice Age patient's pain and bleeding were managed is simply unknown.
Andean surgeons operated on the skull for nearly two thousand years, with survival improving over time. No written record tells us what, if anything, eased the pain.
In 1804 Hanaoka Seishū used a herbal preparation to anaesthetise a patient fully for breast surgery, the earliest well-documented general anaesthetic.
Four decades later, and with no knowledge of Hanaoka's work, ether was used in Georgia and then demonstrated publicly in Boston. Publicity, not priority, drove its spread.
An 1879 account from Bunyoro describes banana wine used to dull pain during a caesarean section, a reminder that pain control took many forms.
Reliable anaesthesia, together with antisepsis and blood transfusion, made long, complex operations such as heart transplantation possible.

title: Understanding and preventing infection
dek: People learned to block the spread of disease long before they knew what caused it, and identifying germs did not immediately bring cures.

steps.note: Ragusa's 1377 rule separated travellers for 30 days. It worked on observation, centuries before anyone knew about plague bacteria.
Semmelweis's chlorinated-lime handwashing cut maternal deaths in Vienna in 1847, but his colleagues resisted and the practice lapsed.
John Snow linked cholera to a water pump in 1854 while most doctors still blamed foul air. The famous map came after the investigation, not before.
Drawing on Pasteur's work, Lister used carbolic acid to prevent wound infection, turning germ theory into surgical practice.
Laveran found the malaria parasite in Algeria in 1880, the first protozoan shown to cause disease, and was doubted for nearly a decade.
Koch identified the tuberculosis bacillus in 1882, but effective drugs took another sixty years.
Knowing how a disease travels can matter as much as knowing its cause: mosquitoes became the target of malaria control.
Fleming's 1928 observation sat largely unused for a decade until others turned it into a medicine.
A cheap drink of sugar and salt, proven in Dhaka and the 1971 refugee camps, became one of the most effective responses to deadly diarrhoea.

title: Vaccination and disease eradication
dek: Inoculation travelled from Asia and Africa to Europe and the Americas, became vaccination, and eventually ended smallpox.

steps.note: Deliberately giving a mild smallpox infection was practised in China, Africa and the Ottoman world long before Europe adopted it.
In Boston, knowledge from an enslaved African man, Onesimus, led to inoculation and to an early attempt to judge it by counting deaths.
Jenner tested and publicised cowpox, a safer substitute. A Dorset farmer had already tried it on his family.
Vaccine crossed oceans in the bodies of orphaned children, an achievement inseparable from its ethical cost.
Twentieth-century vaccines were tested in trials of unprecedented size, in the United States and, during the Cold War, in the Soviet Union.
Case-finding and containment, not just mass vaccination, ended smallpox. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977.
The same ring strategy was used to test an Ebola vaccine in Guinea during an epidemic.
The first vaccine against a human parasite was recommended in 2021 after pilots led by health ministries in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.
Fifteen years of largely unheralded laboratory work made mRNA vaccines possible within a year of the COVID-19 pandemic's start.

title: Seeing inside the body
dek: From reading signs on the surface to listening, cutting and finally imaging, with long gaps where knowledge was lost or ignored.

steps.note: An Egyptian surgeon described the surface of the brain in skull wounds, recording what injuries revealed.
Babylonian scholars organised diagnosis as a reference work linking outward signs to what was happening within.
Ibn al-Nafis reasoned that blood passes through the lungs, a correct insight forgotten in the West for nearly seven centuries.
Vesalius made dissection and accurate illustration the basis of anatomy, using the bodies of executed criminals.
The stethoscope let doctors hear disease in the chest and check their judgements against autopsy.
X-rays showed the inside of the living body without surgery and were adopted with extraordinary speed.
Computing turned X-rays into slices through the body, revealing soft tissue such as the brain.

title: Making childbirth safer
dek: Knowledge about pregnancy and birth has been written down for nearly 4,000 years; the obstacles have often been secrecy, resistance and access.

steps.note: Egypt's oldest surviving medical papyrus is devoted to women's health, fertility and pregnancy.
A family of London practitioners kept a life-saving instrument secret for over a century.
Handwashing slashed deaths from childbed fever in Vienna, yet the evidence was resisted.
In 1879 a European visitor watched a caesarean in Bunyoro in which mother and child survived, at a time when the operation was often fatal in European hospitals.
A sheep experiment in Auckland led to a randomised trial showing that steroids before birth protect premature babies.
Short of incubators, doctors in Bogotá turned parents' bodies into the incubator. Trials later confirmed the benefit.

title: Caring for the mind
dek: Explanations of mental illness and ways of caring for it, from Greek arguments against divine causes to community care in Belgium and Nigeria.

steps.note: A Greek author insisted that epilepsy had natural causes in the brain, though stigma long outlasted the argument.
Pilgrims seeking cures at Geel were boarded with local families, the start of a tradition of community care that continues today.
Cairo's great hospital included wards for mental illness within a general, endowed institution.
A small uncontrolled study in Melbourne revived lithium, later confirmed by a placebo-controlled trial in Denmark.
At Aro in Nigeria, patients lived in villages during treatment, an influential model of culturally grounded community psychiatry.
